title: Maximum Sum of Distinct Subarrays With Length K
description: Brute force to optimized: rebuilding a duplicate-check set per window versus an incrementally-maintained running sum and frequency map.

content.title: Maximum Sum of Distinct Subarrays With Length K

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, find the maximum subarray sum among all contiguous subarrays of length k that have no duplicate elements. If no such subarray exists, return 0.

blocks.caption: Slide a fixed-size window, only considering windows where every element is distinct

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, find the maximum subarray sum among all contiguous subarrays of length k with no duplicate elements, or 0 if none qualify.

blocks.title: Analogy: Scoring the Best Valid k-Person Team
blocks.text: Like sliding a window over a lineup of players to form every possible team of exactly k consecutive players, but instantly disqualifying any team that happens to include the same player twice.

blocks.caption: Slide the roster window, disqualify any with a repeated member, and score only the valid ones

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The window [4,2,9] (indices 2-4)","sum 15, all distinct","This is the highest-summing window where no value repeats"],["The window [9,9,9] (indices 4-6)","disqualified","Every element is the same value, 9, so it has zero distinct values, not 3"],["Answer","15","The best valid (all-distinct) window found"]]}

blocks.text: The only possible length-3 window is [4,4,4], which has a repeated value, so it is disqualified, leaving no valid window at all, and the answer is 0.
Before checking each window's uniqueness from scratch, notice this builds directly on the fixed-size sliding window shape already used for sums, adding a duplicate-detection layer on top.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: This is a fixed-size sliding window, just like Maximum Average Subarray I, so the running sum can be updated incrementally as the window slides.

Observation 2: A window has no duplicates exactly when the number of DISTINCT values inside it equals its own size, k.

Observation 3: Maintain a frequency map counting how many times each value currently appears within the window, updating it the same way the running sum is updated: add the entering value's count, remove the leaving value's count once it drops to zero.

Observation 4: At every fully-formed window (once at least k elements have been processed), check whether the frequency map's size (the count of distinct values) equals k; only then is the current running sum a valid candidate for the answer.

Combining an incrementally-updated running sum with an incrementally-updated frequency map lets both the sum and the duplicate check be answered in O(1) per slide, instead of rechecking the whole window from scratch.
This "frequency map for validity, alongside a running sum for the value" combination is a common extension of the basic fixed-size sliding window pattern.
For every possible window, check directly whether all k elements are distinct, and if so, compute its sum.

items: For every possible starting position, extract the length-k window and check whether it contains any duplicate values, using a set.
If the window has no duplicates, compute its sum directly and compare it against the best sum found so far.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A fresh set is built for every window, since duplicate-checking needs to be independent for each candidate window.
The sum and the duplicate check are both computed within the same single pass over the current window, rather than two separate passes.
best starts at 0 rather than negative infinity, since the problem explicitly asks for 0 when no valid window exists at all.

blocks.text: Every window's true distinctness and sum are computed directly, so the correct maximum is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * k), since each of the roughly n windows is rebuilt and rechecked from scratch.
Space: O(k) for the temporary set used per window.
Limitation: rebuilding a fresh set and re-summing k elements for every one of the roughly n windows repeats almost all of the same work across neighboring windows, since they share k-1 elements.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force rebuilds duplicate-detection state from scratch for every window, discarding almost all of it between neighboring windows that share k-1 elements. Instead, maintain a frequency map alongside the running sum, both updated the same way as the window slides: add the entering value's contribution, remove the leaving value's contribution. A window has no duplicates exactly when the frequency map's size (its count of distinct values) equals k, letting the duplicate check become an O(1) size comparison instead of rebuilding a set from scratch.

Slide a window of size k across nums, maintaining both a running sum and a frequency map of values currently in the window. At every fully-formed window, check whether the frequency map has exactly k distinct keys; if so, the window has no duplicates, and its running sum is a valid candidate for the answer.
Maintain a running sum and a frequency map together, both updated incrementally as the window slides one position at a time.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass.
Space: O(k), for the frequency map, which holds at most k entries at any time.

The running sum updates the same way as in any fixed-size sliding window: subtract the leaving value, add the entering value. The frequency map tracks exactly how many times each value currently appears within the window; its size (the number of distinct keys) can only ever be at most k, and it equals k precisely when every one of the k elements in the window is a different value, since duplicates would collapse two or more positions onto the same key.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Distinct count vs k","Meaning"],"rows":[["Distinct count equals k","Every element in the window is unique","Window is valid, consider its sum"],["Distinct count is less than k","At least one value repeats within the window","Window is invalid, skip it"]]}

items: The running sum and the frequency map are updated together, in lockstep, every time the window slides.

A value is removed from the frequency map entirely once its count drops to zero, rather than left in the map with a zero count, since the map's SIZE (distinct count) is what the validity check relies on.
The validity and sum checks only happen once the window has reached its full size of k elements (guarded by the index check), never on a partially-formed window.

blocks.text: This problem extends the basic fixed-size sliding window pattern by adding an incrementally-maintained frequency map, letting both the running sum and the duplicate-detection check update in O(1) per slide.

items: Leaving a value in the frequency map with a count of 0 instead of removing it entirely, which would incorrectly inflate the distinct-count check.
Checking window validity before the window has actually reached its full size of k elements, producing false positives on partially-formed windows.
Rebuilding the frequency map from scratch on every slide instead of updating it incrementally, losing the O(n) time improvement.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Every length-k window has at least one duplicate","Correctly returns 0, since no window is ever valid"],["All elements in nums are already distinct","Every window is valid, and the answer is simply the maximum window sum"]]}

items: Explicitly connect this back to the basic fixed-size sliding window pattern, describing the frequency map as an additional piece of incrementally-maintained state, not a fundamentally different technique.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find the best sum over every FIXED-size window, but only windows with NO duplicate elements count" points toward a fixed-size sliding window with an added frequency map tracking distinct-value counts.

items: How would this change if the window size k could vary, rather than being fixed? A variable-size sliding window would be needed, growing or shrinking based on both the target size and the duplicate condition.
What if you needed the actual subarray, not just its sum? Track the best starting index alongside the best sum, updating both together whenever a new best valid window is found.

How would you count the total number of valid (duplicate-free) length-k windows, rather than find the best sum? The same frequency map check applies, just incrementing a counter instead of tracking a maximum sum.
Directly extends the fixed-size sliding window sum technique from Maximum Average Subarray I, adding a frequency map for duplicate detection.
The "frequency map whose size indicates validity" technique reappears in Subarrays with K Different Integers, applied there to variable-size windows instead of fixed-size ones.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n * k) time, O(k) space.
Optimized (incremental sum + frequency map): O(n) time, O(k) space.

items: Pattern: Fixed-size sliding window with an incrementally-maintained frequency map for duplicate detection
Core Idea: A window has no duplicates exactly when its frequency map's distinct-value count equals the window size k
Time: O(n)
Space: O(k)
Most Important Observation: Both the running sum and the duplicate check can be maintained incrementally in lockstep as the window slides, avoiding any full window rebuild
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Slide the sum and the frequency map together; valid exactly when distinct count equals k
